subtype: Approach: taking any offer without thinking [Pitfall]
passage:
“You look awful,” Eshaan said, dropping his bag next to Sarika in the corridor.
“Two nights. Don't start.”
“Two nights of what?”
“Deliveries. After ten. A man from a group chat offered it, no forms, no questions. Easy money.”
“And the maths test you slept through?”
“It's one test.”
“What was in the bags?”
Sarika looked at the floor. “He said not to open them.”
“Did he pay you?”
“Friday. He promised.”
“Last night, what happened?”
“A car kept slowing beside me. I dumped the bags at the tea stall and ran.” Her hands were shaking now.
“Then he's not paying you Friday. Come on, we're telling the counsellor. Right now.”
Sarika nodded. At the office the counsellor looked up, saw her face and said, “Sit down. You're not in trouble.”

qa.q: How many nights had Sarika delivered bags?
What might Sarika be feeling as she describes the car?
qa.a: Fear: her hands are shaking as she admits she ran, which shows the easy money no longer feels safe.

qa.q: What should Sarika have done before accepting, and why?
qa.a: She should have asked who the man was, what was in the bags and the exact hours, and told a parent or teacher first, because vague terms and night work for a school student are warning signs.

qa.q: How does the job look to Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan sees a stranger handing a schoolmate unknown bags at night, so he worries about her safety and wants a trusted adult involved straight away.

grounding: A student takes a night delivery job with vague terms, and it proves unsafe and clashes with school.
